walkthroughs.body_html:
On the Wild Side — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

On the Wild Side brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with On the Wild Side.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How does myelination increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction?
options: Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.
Myelin makes the axon thicker so the signal travels faster through more material.
Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), skipping the myelinated sections.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.

mcqs.q: How does sweating help cool you down?
options: Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Evaporation of sweat absorbs energy (latent heat) from the skin, lowering body temperature.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.
Sweat is cold and directly cools the skin on contact.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Ester bond”?
options: Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Hydrolysis”?
options: Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Monomer”?
options: Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Polymer”?
options: Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Glycosidic bond”?
options: Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Condensation reaction”?
options: Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
